name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,842

clue.text: Salt absorbed by exposed sticker on hull? (8)

indicators.note: What a material absorbs is taken up inside it, so the piece named first ends up within the word that soaks it up.

blocks.note: an exposed stretch of hull is a bare one
NaCl is the chemical formula of common salt, sodium chloride

explanation.surface: Sea salt soaking into a label stuck on a bare patch of a ship's hull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' is the crossword's usual old sailor for one reading and a chemistry lesson for the other; only the formula gives letters. The question mark owns up to 'sticker' being a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A barnacle cements itself to a ship's bottom and will not come off, so 'sticker' is plain English for what it does.

clue.text: Quickly take off clothes rolling about (5)

indicators.note: A garment goes round the person wearing it, so as a verb the word tells one piece to wrap itself about another.
Something rolling comes round to face the other way, so the two letters are written in the reverse order.

blocks.note: to ape a person is to take them off, imitating their manner
about is ca, short for the Latin circa, and it arrives turned round

explanation.surface: A frantic scramble out of one's clothes, rolling around on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is about undressing: 'take off' is an impersonation and 'clothes' is an instruction. CA for 'about' is the circa you meet in front of uncertain dates.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that proceeds apace proceeds quickly — the adverb survives mainly in that one phrase.

clue.text: Hearing of stolen rowing boat, wink (7)

indicators.note: To hear of a thing is to meet it by ear, so what follows is to be judged by its sound rather than its spelling.

blocks.note: to nick something is British slang for stealing it
an eight is the long racing boat rowed by a crew of eight

explanation.surface: On hearing that a racing boat has been stolen, someone gives a knowing wink.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'eight' is a boat before it is a number, which is the step most solvers miss. Run the two spoken words together and the join between them falls in a different place from the join between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: To nictate is to blink or wink: the technical verb for what an eyelid does, borrowed from the nictitating membrane.

clue.text: Elderly people in care got involved in cryonics, perhaps (4,7)

indicators.note: People who get involved in something are mixed up in it, and letters mixed up do not come out in the order they were handed over.

blocks.note: the olds is informal British for the older generation
seven more letters for the mixture, with 'in' only joining them on

explanation.surface: Pensioners in a care home signing up for some cryonics experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture the surface paints — old people frozen for later — is exactly what the answer describes, so the definition hides in plain sight. 'Got' looks like part of the instruction and is really more fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryonics is the freezing of bodies in hope of later revival, which makes it one particular use of cold storage.

clue.text: Register concerning gut (7)

blocks.note: to register a name is to enter it in the book
a book on Rome is a book concerning Rome

explanation.surface: A record kept on the subject of somebody's digestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' for 'concerning' is the preposition of book titles and lecture notices, and it slips past because the clue reads like a line from a medical file.
explanation.definitionFit: The enteron is the alimentary canal, the zoologist's word for the gut from one end to the other.

clue.text: Religious statue friend had wobbled (6)

indicators.note: A thing that wobbles will not stay put, and letters that will not stay put settle in a different order.

blocks.note: bud is American-flavoured slang for a pal
the three letters of the word, shaken up

explanation.surface: A friend who had a wobble in front of a religious statue.
explanation.walkthrough: The word does double service, naming the Enlightened One and any of the seated figures of him, which is what lets 'statue' define it.
explanation.definitionFit: A buddha is not only the teacher but any image of him seated cross-legged, the ornament sold in every gift shop.

clue.text: Extra run later (3)

blocks.note: the cricket sense: an extra is a run the batter never touched, and this is the kind that slips past the wicketkeeper
the parting word, said as you go

explanation.surface: A cricket scorer's note about an extra run to be added later.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an extra is any run not scored off the bat, and this one is credited when the ball beats both batter and keeper. The farewell sense is the other half.
explanation.definitionFit: A bye is the cricket extra run taken when nobody touches the ball, and 'bye' is also the casual goodbye that 'later' stands in for.

clue.text: Middle of tour through Leeds strangely free from nippers (7)

indicators.note: The middle of a four-letter word is the pair standing in the centre, one letter trimmed from each side.
Something driven through a thing passes into its body, so these letters land inside the others rather than beside them.
Letters behaving strangely are not behaving as given, so they arrive in another order.

blocks.note: the five letters of the Yorkshire city, rearranged
the two letters at the centre of the word

explanation.surface: The middle leg of a tour through Leeds, oddly free of small children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nippers' is British for small children on the surface and biting insects underneath, so the definition is a job of work rather than a happy coincidence. The city is there for its letters alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To delouse is to rid a person or a place of lice, and lice are nippers in the literal sense — they bite.

clue.text: Utility, one of no fixed address next to banks? (9)

definitions.text: Utility, one of no fixed address next to banks?

indicators.note: Banks are what a river runs between, so as a verb the word has the outer pieces close along either side of what sits between them.

blocks.note: a hobo is a wanderer with nowhere to call home
at the door, at the bar: at puts you next to a thing
the utility of a thing is its use

explanation.surface: A homeless man dossing down next to the banks in the high street.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice, as description and as instruction, which is why nothing is left over for a separate definition. 'Banks' pulls you towards the high street and is really the wrapper.
explanation.definitionFit: The sentence reads straight: a useful thing with no address to give, moored against the banks of a river rather than standing in a street.

clue.text: Third guy like the Gallagher brothers? (4)

blocks.note: a guy is a man
label them A, B and C, and the third one is C

explanation.surface: Picking out the third bloke in a line-up as another of the Gallagher sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel and Liam Gallagher of Oasis are Manchester's most famous sons and have never let anyone forget it, so the definition is a demonym rather than a description of how they behave.
explanation.definitionFit: A Manc is a Mancunian, someone from Manchester, which is where the brothers grew up and where the accent comes from.

clue.text: Young darts player taking 50 to finish eliminated untidy thrower (6,4)

indicators.note: To take a thing is to lift it out of where it sits, so the numeral leaves the name it was standing in.
The finish is the far end, which is where the lifted letter is set back down.

blocks.note: Luke Littler is the teenage darts champion; this is his surname once the numeral below has been lifted out of it
L is fifty in Roman numerals
a player eliminated from a tournament is out

explanation.surface: A teenage darts player takes the bullseye to check out, and is knocked out of the tournament anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: Luke Littler reached a world final at sixteen, which is what turns 'young darts player' into a name. The 50 is a bullseye on the surface and a Roman numeral underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter lout is the person who drops rubbish in the street, so the definition names the habit by the throwing it involves.

clue.text: Years with Labour deliver peanuts, unfortunately (5,9)

indicators.note: What happens unfortunately has gone wrong, and letters that go wrong come out in the wrong order.

blocks.note: fourteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Years of Labour government that end up paying derisory wages.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter drags 'Labour' towards the party and 'peanuts' towards poor pay, while the definition wants hard labour and a long stretch inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Penal servitude was the formal sentence of imprisonment with hard labour, so years spent at that labour is precisely what it means.

clue.text: Trinity Lane turns the way one travels (11)

indicators.note: A thing that turns comes round differently, so the letters are set down in another order.

blocks.note: eleven letters, and a real street: Trinity Lane runs beside Trinity College in Cambridge

explanation.surface: A Cambridge lane bending round in the direction a traveller is heading.
explanation.walkthrough: A lane that 'turns' reads as a bend in the road, and the definition reads as the rest of the direction; both are doing quite different work.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lives itinerantly moves from place to place, so the adverb names the manner of a traveller's life.

clue.text: Incredibly rainy round part of Johannesburg (6)

blocks.note: so wet, so tired: so is the everyday intensifier
a rainy day is a wet one
a round is drawn as a circle, the letter O

explanation.surface: Torrential weather parked over one district of Johannesburg.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is a contraction of South Western Townships, the sprawl on Johannesburg's edge that became part of the city, so the definition is geography and not weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Soweto is the vast township on the south-western side of Johannesburg and has been within the city's boundary since 2002.

clue.text: Where bandage goes, too tight? (9)

blocks.note: the answer to where a dressing sits is over the thing it protects
the place a bandage goes is an injury

explanation.surface: A dressing put on the injury, and pulled far too tight.
explanation.walkthrough: The seam hides a change of sense: one of those two words is an injury and the other is the past of wind, and only the second gives a spring turned too far.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch or a spring wound past its limit is overwound, which is exactly what being too tight amounts to.

clue.text: World's longest river crossing a mafia boss guaranteed (6-2)

indicators.note: One thing crossing another cuts into it, so the letter lands inside the name rather than after it.

blocks.note: the Nile, some 6,650 km from source to delta
the single letter, taken as it stands
a don is the head of a mafia family

explanation.surface: A mob boss crossing the Nile, with safe passage promised.
explanation.walkthrough: Whether the Nile or the Amazon is the longer river is disputed by geographers, but crosswords have settled on the Nile. The definition is sports-page English.
explanation.definitionFit: Nailed-on is British sporting slang for a certainty: a nailed-on penalty is one nobody in the ground disputes.

clue.text: Mould encountered around dish (8)

indicators.note: Something brought around comes to face the other way, so the word just clued is written from its last letter back.

blocks.note: encountered is met, turned round
a dish on the table is a plate

explanation.surface: Fungus found growing around an unwashed dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words mislead at once: 'mould' is the shaping pattern rather than the stuff on the plate, and 'around' turns the first piece instead of wrapping it round anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A template is the shape you cut round or copy from, doing for a cut-out what a mould does for anything cast in it.

clue.text: Fit as a golfer wants to be? There's a moral in that (7)

definitions.note: The definition is a whole sentence where the answer is a noun: the setter points at the thing with 'that' and tells you what is inside it, which is how a story of this kind is described rather than named.

blocks.clueFragment: as a golfer wants to be
blocks.note: par is the target score, and on par is where every golfer wants to be
fit for a task means able to do it

explanation.surface: Being in the shape every golfer dreams of, with a lesson to be drawn from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' is the adjective of capability, not of health, and the golf is there only because par is the number a round is measured against. Read the halves together and the wordplay is a golfer's boast.
explanation.definitionFit: A parable is a short story told to carry a lesson, so pointing at one and saying there is a moral in it describes it exactly.

clue.text: American, say, bungling start of hit single (7)

indicators.note: A bungled job comes out wrong, and letters bungled come out in an order nobody intended.
The start of a word is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
six more letters for the mixture, the whole word this time

explanation.surface: An American singer fluffing the opening of a hit single.
explanation.walkthrough: A comma and 'say' usually mean you are being handed an example of the answer rather than a synonym for it, and here the example is one national variety of a language.
explanation.definitionFit: American English is one of the language's national forms, so American is an example of the answer and 'say' flags it as one.

clue.text: Wake partner before call (6)

blocks.note: an ex is a partner from before
to cite a witness is to call them

explanation.surface: Waking your partner before the phone call comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' has to be read as rousing something abstract rather than shaking a sleeper, and 'call' is the summons of a courtroom, not the telephone the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: You wake an interest or a suspicion exactly as you excite one: both verbs take a dormant feeling and bring it to life.

clue.text: Mark removed from 18 façade? (7)

blocks.note: the surface offers a stain being scrubbed off the front of number 18
18 down is ENGLISH, and English writes this French word without the little hook under its c

explanation.surface: A stain being cleaned off the frontage of number 18.
explanation.walkthrough: The 18 is a cross-reference to 18 down rather than a house number, and the clue prints the word with its hook still in place so you can see what English drops.
explanation.definitionFit: A cedilla is the tail written under a c to soften it, and since English spells facade without one it is the mark English removes.

clue.text: Henry hides uranium in network of tunnels protecting US president (6,1,7)

indicators.note: To hide a thing is to cover it over, so one of the two letters named goes out of sight and the other is what you see in its place.

blocks.note: a warren is the network of tunnels a rabbit colony digs
protecting is guarding, and that is the word the swap happens inside
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
uranium is U, the letter that disappears under the henry

explanation.surface: A spy stashing uranium in the tunnel network that shields the president.
explanation.walkthrough: Two scientific symbols do the work, one stepping into the other's place inside a long word. Warren Gamaliel Harding won the White House in 1920 and died in office three years later.
explanation.definitionFit: Warren G Harding was the twenty-ninth president of the United States, and the middle initial is part of how he is always named.

clue.text: Macaroni cheese sandwiches not appealing to many (5)

indicators.note: A sandwich keeps its filling out of sight between two slices, so what is wanted is already buried inside the words as written.

blocks.note: the run of letters bridges the join between the two words

explanation.surface: Macaroni cheese served between two slices of bread, which few would want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' works twice over, as lunch on the surface and as the hiding place underneath. Macaroni cheese is British comfort food, and putting it in a sandwich is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche product is aimed at one small slice of the market rather than the crowd, so it appeals to few by design.

clue.text: Hooker's top right behind wig next to his pants (5,5)

indicators.note: What is behind the rest comes last, so the two letters named are parked at the very end.
Pants is British slang for rubbish, and a rubbish arrangement of letters is not the arrangement you were given.

blocks.note: a rug is a toupee
standing by something is standing next to it
the three letters of the word, rearranged
Rt is the abbreviation in Rt Hon, for Right Honourable

explanation.surface: A hooker's top sitting right behind a wig, next to his terrible trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: The hooker of the definition is the forward who wins the ball in the middle of the front row, not the one the surface invites you to picture. 'Pants' is rubbish before it is trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooker packs down in a rugby front row, and the numbered jersey he plays in is a rugby shirt.

clue.text: Watch showing seconds in useless jewelled semicircle (3)

indicators.note: The seconds of a run of words are the letters standing second in each of them, taken one word at a time.

blocks.note: the second letter of the word
the second letter of the word
the second letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wristwatch with its seconds shown in a pointless jewelled half-circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' is the verb here rather than the thing on the wrist, and 'seconds' is a counting instruction rather than the sweep hand; the three ornamental words exist only to be counted into.
explanation.definitionFit: Watch the birds, see the birds: in the sense of taking something in with the eyes the two verbs swap freely.

clue.text: Lap speed (4)

blocks.note: what a cat does to a saucer of milk, tongue first
the sense in 'going at a fair old one' — a rate of knots

explanation.surface: A question about how fast one circuit of the track was.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words are enough to build a motor-racing picture, and both of them turn out to belong to the tongue and the open road instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat laps milk by licking it, and 'at a fair old lick' is everyday British for at considerable speed.

clue.text: Stick together fellow admitted by doctor in A&E (6)

indicators.note: A patient admitted by a hospital is taken inside it, so the piece goes within the word that admits it.
In puts the assembled piece between the two letters standing either side of it.

blocks.note: A&E is how British hospitals signpost accident and emergency, and those are its two letters with the ampersand dropped
dr is the everyday abbreviation
a fellow is a he

explanation.surface: A man brought into casualty by the doctor on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: One insertion sits inside another, the casualty department being the outer wrapper. 'Stick together' is glue and sticking plaster rather than solidarity, which is what the hospital surface wants you to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Two surfaces that adhere stick together and stay stuck, which is what glue, tape and a plaster are all for.

clue.text: Silly malarkey making large hot punch (8)

indicators.note: Letters behaving sillily are not behaving as given, so they end up in another order.
Making one thing into another puts the second in the first's place, so the letter named second joins the mixture and the first drops out.

blocks.note: the word's letters with the L lifted out
large is L, the letter that goes
H is hot, as marked on a tap, and it takes the L's place

explanation.surface: Daft nonsense that ends up producing a big bowl of hot punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' is the party bowl on the surface and a blow underneath. The blow takes its name from the wide swing of a scythe through hay, which has nothing to do with the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A haymaker is a wild swinging blow thrown to knock someone out, named for the sweep of a scythe at harvest.
